accuracy.evidence: Checked against the NHS sun safety page (shade 11am to 3pm March to October in the UK, cover up with clothes, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses, SPF 30 or more with 4 or 5 star UVA, reapply after swimming or towel drying and about every 2 hours, extra care for ears, neck and tops of feet), the WHO 2002 UV Index guide (thin cloud lets most UV through, UV peaks near solar noon) and the EPA SunWise shadow rule. The lab sun peaks at 60 degrees, as on a UK summer day, and a shadow is shorter than the child only above 45 degrees, roughly 10:45am to 3:15pm, matching the 11 to 3 advice.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented beliefs that a cloudy, cool or breezy day is safe and that you cannot burn in water (heat is not UV), that a cap is enough, that a vest top or swimsuit is enough cover, that ears, neck, hands and feet do not need cream, and that one morning application lasts all day; each appears as a wrong option with its own reply and in the adult common mistakes.

lab_distinct.evidence: Only this topic uses a draggable sun whose height sets a child's shadow beside a dashed line as tall as the child, a heat meter that falls while a UV meter stays up, clothes dragged onto a child, tap targets on bare skin patches, and a sun cream meter that drains after a swim. It is about skin protection, not eyes (flagsunsafe) or warming (flagsun).

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the shadow rule by dragging the sun until the shadow falls short of the dashed line, sees with the meters that cool does not mean less UV, finds that a cap, vest and swimsuit are refused with the skin they leave bare, and sees the cream meter drop after swimming; the step text then names each rule.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: the sun is strongest in the morning when it is low (the dragged sun shows the short midday shadow and strong UV), a cloudy cool day cannot burn (the UV meter stays high under cloud), and sun cream lasts all day after a swim (the cream meter shows it rubbed off).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions; wrong options carry tags with distinct replies: cool (UV not heat burns, and it passes through cloud and breeze), cap (ears and neck left bare), vest (shoulders burn fast), swim (lots of bare skin), covered (cream goes on bare skin), allday and wait (cream wears off), face (one patch only), hatonly and sunrun.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and everyday words (shadow, shade, sun cream, bare skin) and scores far below the family kid limit; adult text scores FK 8.4 and defines UV, SPF and the shadow rule in plain words.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph gives one rule (UV burns unseen, the shadow rule, cool is not safe, cover up and cream); adult paragraphs give the DfE requirement, the NHS and EPA advice with numbers, the mistakes, and the lab walk-through, with no repeated wording.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark checked: the sun and tree scene fills the width, the clothes grid sits beside the child in two columns with labels shortened so none clip (Wide brim hat), cream targets are at least 44 px, the day scene was enlarged, and tray buttons wrap cleanly at 390 px.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a tray button (earlier, later, go into the shade, each weather change, each piece of clothing, each skin patch, each choice); the canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action; the shadow was darkened for the dark theme; walk.cjs runs axe in both themes on desktop and phone.

sources: DfE (2019) Relationships Education, RSE and Health Education statutory guidance: Physical health and mental wellbeing, Health and prevention (safe and unsafe exposure to the sun, reducing the risk of sun damage including skin cancer)
NHS: Sunscreen and sun safety (shade 11am to 3pm, cover up, SPF 30+, 4 or 5 star UVA, reapply after swimming and about every 2 hours)
World Health Organization (2002) Global Solar UV Index: A Practical Guide
US EPA SunWise programme: the shadow rule (if your shadow is shorter than you, UV is strong)
